confirmed.title: POSIX hang dump: a reply that arrives after the 1 s timeout is counted for the next thread, and its handler can write stack lines into a reused fd such as the next standalone_boot_state.txt
confirmed.bug_class: wait without matching wakeup / fd use after close across threads
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.repro_idea: In a Linux attended run (BANISHED_UNATTENDED unset), hold the main thread past 20 s while another thread sits inside dlopen, for example with an LD_PRELOAD'ed constructor that sleeps 2 s. Then check standalone_hang.log for mismatched or duplicated thread sections and look for '#N' frame lines in standalone_boot_state.txt. Fixes: give each request its own sequence number (the handler posts only if its sequence matches) and make g_hangLog atomic, leaving the fd open until every pending handler has answered.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: low (diagnostic output only; attended Linux/Android hang dump)
verdict.proof:
The code in <worktree>/src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp matches the finding, and the finding is not in the ledger. README.md, findings_p3p4.json and findings_p8.json have no hit for hang dump, sem_timedwait, g_hangLog or kDumpSignal. P0_MAP.md:438 lists the watchdog only for its Interlocked flags. No origin/main commit touches this logic.

What the code shows:
(1) One sem_t g_dumpDone (:96) is shared by every request, and nothing identifies which request a reply belongs to. When sem_timedwait (:201) times out, it does not cancel the signal already sent by tgkill (:194). If that handler runs DumpOwnStack and reaches sem_post (:147) after the timeout, the post stays in the semaphore. The next thread's wait then returns at once, so replies are attributed to the wrong thread from that point on. The late handler's frame lines also interleave with the header of the next thread (:187), because the watchdog keeps writing the log while the handler writes it.
(2) g_hangLog is a plain int. The handlers read it at :100 and :110, and the watchdog thread writes it at :153 and :210 with no synchronisation, which is a formal data race. Close-then-reuse is possible: a handler can pass the `g_hangLog < 0` check, the watchdog can then run close() (:209), and the following write() goes to whatever has reused that fd number. On an attended run (no _exit(4) at :262), the next fd allocated is the fopen of standalone_boot_state.txt in WriteStateFile (:84), about one second later. On an unattended run, _exit(4) follows at once and that path is gone.

Why it is not confirmed:
- The trigger needs a handler that takes longer than 1 s and then finishes. dladdr takes the dynamic-linker lock. If the hung thread holds that lock forever, the handler never posts, so no stray post is produced. The stray-post case needs the lock to be held for a bounded time over 1 s, or slow O_SYNC writes of up to 40 lines.
- The fd-reuse path is narrower still. A handler must be between the check at :100 and the write at :101 across the close at :209 and the next fopen.
- No test, sanitizer report or repro exists.

The structural defect can be checked line by line: there is no per-request sequence number and no wait for late answers before close. The observable damage needs a run, for example an attended Linux run with a thread held in dlopen for 2 s, as the finding suggests. The Android twin is cited at :212-219 and was not re-read. This affects only the harness and diagnostics. It has no sim or save impact.
verdict.minimal_fix: Give each request a sequence number. Keep a std::atomic<uint32_t> g_dumpSeq: the watchdog increments it before tgkill, and the handler copies its value on entry and posts only if it still matches. Better, replace the post with an atomic ack counter that the watchdog compares with the expected sequence. Make g_hangLog std::atomic<int> (lock-free, so it is signal-safe). Before close(), give late handlers a short drain: wait until an in-flight counter (incremented on handler entry, decremented on exit) reaches 0, or keep the hang-log fd open (or dup2 it to /dev/null) instead of closing it, so a late write cannot reach a reused fd. Apply the same fix to src/diag/android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp (and to the Darwin twin if it has the same structure).

proof_run.proof:
The finding is confirmed on fa150cf7f (the same as origin/main) by a WSL g++ repro and a TSan report. The repro compiles the real src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp into one translation unit, with stubs for Opt() and Cpu, and calls the file's own WriteHangDump. It uses one thread B whose dump signal is delivered after the 1 s timeout (it is masked, then unmasked late), and two threads C and D that never answer.

Run with B answering at +2500 ms (run_2500): the dump shows "(no answer within 1s)" for B and C only. D's section has no "(no answer)" line, and its body holds B's frames ("#4 repro + 0x36A9 (late_answerer_fn+0x89)") under D's header ("--- thread 4391 ---"). So B's late sem_post satisfied D's wait, and the reply was counted for the wrong thread. Result: '(no answer' lines = 2, expected 3. FAIL.

Run with B answering at +3500 ms, after the dump had ended (run_3500): g_dumpDone holds 1 after the dump, a stray post. In the next WriteHangDump that post is consumed by the first thread, so the attribution shifts: '(no answer' lines = 1, expected 2. FAIL.

The same repro built with -fsanitize=thread (run_tsan_3500/tsan.txt) gives "WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race". It is a read of g_hangLog in HangLogRaw (boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp:100, called from DumpOwnStack and DumpSignalHandler on the late thread) against the earlier write at :153 in WriteHangDump on the watchdog thread. A second race is on the fd itself: write() at :101 against open() at :153. In that run the late handler wrote its stack into the NEXT dump's log file.

Not observed: stack lines landing in a reused fd such as standalone_boot_state.txt. That needs a handler preempted between the check at :100 and the write at :101 across close() at :209, a window too narrow to force. That sub-claim is still a consequence of the data race TSan proved, not an observed write.

src/diag/android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp has the identical structure at :89-106 and :171-228: a shared sem, sem_timedwait, then close and g_hangLog = -1. It was not run.

This affects harness and diagnostic output only, with no sim or save impact. No changes were made in the worktree.
proof_run.minimal_fix:
In both src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp and src/diag/android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp:

1. Make g_hangLog a std::atomic<int>. It is lock-free, so it is safe to read in a signal handler. The handler loads it once per line.
2. Add a std::atomic<uint32_t> g_dumpSeq and a std::atomic<uint32_t> g_dumpAck. The watchdog stores ++seq before tgkill. The handler reads seq on entry, dumps, then stores ack = seq and calls sem_post. After sem_timedwait the watchdog accepts the reply only if ack == the expected seq, and otherwise drains stale posts with sem_trywait and keeps waiting until the deadline. Before each tgkill it also clears leftover posts with a sem_trywait loop.
3. Do not let a late handler write into a reused fd. Before close(), dup2 an fd opened on /dev/null over the hang-log fd, or keep the hang-log fd open for the life of the process, so a late write cannot land in standalone_boot_state.txt.
proof_run.repro_path: scratchpad/phase2/proofs/hangdump-stray-post/ (repro.cpp, run.sh, stubs/, run_output.txt, run_2500/standalone_hang_1.log, run_3500/, run_tsan_3500/tsan.txt)

confirmed.title: DiagThreads: when a thread id is reused, the slot is updated in place behind the sampler's g_seenRegistered cursor, so the new thread is never sampled and role and busy are published as a torn pair
confirmed.bug_class: thread lifecycle / publication without a consistent snapshot
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.repro_idea: Run BANISHED_SAMPLE=1000 across several save/load or world-reload cycles. Grep standalone_samples.txt for '@S' or '@P' lines after the second world; a reused tid shows none even though that thread ran. A unit test can register thread A, record Count(), let A exit and register thread B with A's tid forced through a fake CurrentThreadId, and show that the sampler-side scan from the old cursor never yields B.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: logic (diag only, BANISHED_SAMPLE profile loses a thread; no sim/save effect)
verdict.proof:
Static reasoning, line by line, on origin/main (<worktree>).
1) src/diag/diag_threads.cpp:38-43: Register() calls FindSlot(tid). On a hit it stores busy then role into the existing slot and returns. g_count does not grow and tid is not republished.
2) src/diag/win/sampler.cpp:178-197: RefreshTracked() reads only indices in [g_seenRegistered, Count()) and moves g_seenRegistered forward past each one (line 185). Nothing else reads the registry, and the cursor never moves back. A slot updated in place below the cursor is never read again.
3) sampler.cpp:202-209: WantSample() marks the old Tracked entry dead and closes its own handle once the old thread object is signalled. No code path opens a handle for the new thread that has the same tid. Even if the sampler re-read the slot, line 189 matches only entries where !t.dead.
4) Precondition: Windows frees a thread id only after the last handle to the thread object closes. The sampler closes its handle within one tick of the exit (step 3), so the precondition holds whenever the engine's own System::Thread handle has also been released. The id can then go to a later thread, for example the next per-save PersistenceWorker or a restarted path pool thread. That thread runs RegisterNamed -> Register, hits branch 1 and is never sampled. Every step is visible in the two files. Reuse timing comes from the OS, so a test needs the fake-CurrentThreadId route the finding suggests, but the logic defect does not depend on timing.
Torn pair: the two release stores (busy, then role) are not one atomic snapshot, so RoleAt/BusyAt can pair a new busy with an old role. This half is minor. The sampler never re-reads that slot, and RoleOf reads only role. It is real but has no practical effect.
Not a duplicate: S-034 (README.md:307, findings_p8.json:3021) is the dangling &_runFlags busy pointer kept after a Thread object is freed. This finding is the missed re-registration under the cursor, a separate defect, though a fix for one should take the other into account. Nothing in the ledger mentions tid reuse or g_seenRegistered.
verdict.minimal_fix: In DiagThreads::Register, drop the in-place update. Always append a new slot (fetch_add, store role and busy, then publish tid last), so the sampler's cursor reaches it and RefreshTracked opens a handle for the new owner. Change FindSlot to scan from the newest slot (i = lim-1 down to 0) so RoleOf returns the current owner's role. Slots are still bounded by kMaxThreads. Coordinate with the S-034 fix (forget or clear the slot's busy pointer at thread exit).

confirmed.title: AUTOMENU_CLICKS row guard misses the move-up / move-down neighbour index: token 2000 (row 0) or 3000+last row passes the guard and Modification::Swap indexes _mods[-1] / _mods[count]
confirmed.bug_class: hostile-input / out-of-bounds index (incomplete guard)
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: autostart.cpp:353-361: `if (dlg && id >= 1000 && id < 6000) { const int rows = modDlg->entries.GetSize(); const int row = id % 1000; if (row >= rows) { ... dlg = nullptr; } }` checks only `row`. ModDialog::OnElementEvent (src/game/Dialog/moddialog.cpp:681-692) then runs `modification->Swap(id - 2000, id - 2001)` for 2000-2999 and `Swap(id - 3000, id - 2999)` for 3000-3999. Modification::Swap (src/engine/io/modification.cpp:644-651) is bounds-free, so `RtIO::Mod tmp(_mods._data[a]); _mods._data[a] = _mods._data[b]; _mods._data[b] = tmp;`. Token 2000 with one mod installed passes the guard (row 0 < 1) and calls Swap(0,-1), a read and a write at _mods._data[-1]. Token 3000+(rows-1) calls Swap(rows-1, rows), one element past the end. The real UI has no element that can send these ids, so the guard is the only protection. It was added for exactly this class of fabricated click and covers only the row itself.
confirmed.repro_idea: With one .pkm installed in WinData: BANISHED_AUTOMENU_BUTTON=7 BANISHED_AUTOMENU_CLICKS=2000 (or 3000). Under ASan (WSL Linux build) the result is a heap-buffer-overflow in Modification::Swap. Unit-level check: a ModDialog with 1 entry and OnElementEvent(…, 0x12, 2000, …).

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: memory (harness-only: heap out-of-bounds read and write, reachable only through the BANISHED_AUTOMENU_CLICKS driver)
verdict.proof:
The finding holds when the code is read line by line in <worktree> on origin/main.

1. src/diag/autostart.cpp:353-362. For 1000 <= id < 6000 the guard computes only `row = id % 1000` and skips the click only when `row >= entries.GetSize()`. It never checks the neighbour index that the move-up and move-down arms use.

2. src/game/Dialog/moddialog.cpp:681-692 (ModDialog::OnElementEvent).
   - For ids 2000-2999 it calls `modification->Swap(id - 2000, id - 2001)`.
   - For ids 3000-3999 it calls `Swap(id - 3000, id - 2999)`.
   - Neither call has a bounds check.

3. The dialog builds exactly one entry per mod (moddialog.cpp:~380-403 appends a row for each mod; RefreshDisplay walks `i < modification->GetCount()` and indexes `entries._data[i]`). So the entry count the guard reads equals `_mods` count.

4. src/engine/io/modification.cpp:644-651 (Modification::Swap). The only early return is `if (a == b) return;`. Otherwise it copies `_mods._data[a]`, assigns `_mods._data[a] = _mods._data[b]` and assigns `_mods._data[b] = tmp`. There is no bounds check, which is faithful to retail 0x1800b0xxx as the port's own comment documents.

Failure cases:
- Token 2000 with N >= 1 rows: row 0 < N, so the guard passes. Swap(0, -1) then reads `_data[-1]` and writes a 0x80-byte Mod there. That write lands below the heap block, on allocator metadata.
- Token 3000 + (N-1): row N-1 < N, so the guard passes. Swap(N-1, N) then reads and writes `_data[N]`. That is past the end unless capacity happens to be larger, and even then it is an uninitialized Mod object.

The real UI cannot send these ids: retail only builds the elements that exist, and Swap's lack of bounds checks is retail behaviour. So this is a defect in the harness guard (label harness), not port drift. It is reachable only through BANISHED_AUTOMENU_BUTTON/CLICKS.

The ledger was checked: docs/history/review_20261103 (README, P0_MAP, findings_p3p4.json and findings_p8.json) has no entry for autostart, AUTOMENU_CLICKS or ModDialog Swap, so this is not a duplicate. The code is unchanged on origin/main.

confirmed.title: PAUSEMENU_CLICKS bare <id> token reaches ModDialog::ToggleMod / Swap / ShowDetails with no row bound (the guard autostart.cpp has is missing here)
confirmed.bug_class: hostile-input / out-of-bounds index
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: pausemenu_harness.cpp:186-197: `ModDialog* dlg = ModDialog_LastOpened(); int id = std::atoi(tok); ... if (dlg) { ... static_cast<UI::DialogInstance*>(dlg)->OnElementEvent(&nullElem, 0x12, id, 0, 0, 0, nullptr); }` has no row check, unlike the `t<row>` token a few lines above (`row >= 0 && row < rows`). It is also unlike autostart.cpp:346-361, whose comment says that with no .pkm installed "the entry array count at +0xC0 is 0 and the row handler faults reading its entry". For id 1000-1999, ModDialog::ToggleMod (moddialog.cpp:459-464) does `const ModDialogEntry& entry = entries._data[index]; ... entry.checkLoaded.Get()` and then `Modification::Enable(index, …)`, which writes `_mods._data[index].enabled` with no bound. The 2000-3999 ids reach the same bounds-free Swap. Note that an over-range *row* needs no hostile value: "1000" is out of range whenever the mods folder is parked, which the gate procedure does.
confirmed.repro_idea: With WinData/*.pkm parked: BANISHED_PAUSEMENU=600 BANISHED_PAUSEMENU_BUTTON=<Mods id> BANISHED_PAUSEMENU_CLICKS=1000. Expect a fault (or an ASan heap-buffer-overflow) in ModDialog::ToggleMod reading entries._data[0] of an empty array.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: low (harness only; the input is a developer-set env var, BANISHED_PAUSEMENU_CLICKS, so there is no shipped or player-reachable path. The out-of-bounds read and write are still real UB and can crash a gate run.)
verdict.proof:
The finding is not in the ledger. A grep of docs/history/review_20261103 (README.md, P0_MAP.md, findings_p3p4.json, findings_p8.json) for pausemenu, PAUSEMENU or ModDialog_LastOpened returns nothing relevant. The single "bare" hit is an unrelated FencedTool proof. The code on origin/main in <worktree> is unchanged.

The chain can be checked line by line:
(1) src/diag/pausemenu_harness.cpp:186-198. The bare-token branch runs `int id = std::atoi(tok);` and then `if (dlg) ... OnElementEvent(&nullElem, 0x12, id, 0, 0, 0, nullptr)`. It checks only that the dialog exists. The `t<row>` branch at :160-172 does check `row >= 0 && row < rows`, where `rows = dlg->entries.GetSize()`.
(2) src/game/Dialog/moddialog.cpp:675-692. The dispatcher routes id 1000-1999 to ToggleMod(id-1000), 2000-2999 to `modification->Swap(id-2000, id-2001)`, 3000-3999 to `Swap(id-3000, id-2999)` and 4000-4999 to MoveToTop. None of these checks a range against the entry count.
(3) moddialog.cpp:459-466. ToggleMod does `entries._data[index]`, then `entry.checkLoaded.Get()->_checked` with no bound and no null test. The function's own comment says "the row's presence is the caller's contract (src/diag/autostart.cpp gates its fabricated clicks on the row count)". The pause-menu harness is a second caller of the same kind and does not keep that contract.
(4) src/engine/io/modification.cpp:626-629 and 644-653. Enable writes `_mods._data[index].enabled`, and Swap copies `_mods._data[a]` and `_mods._data[b]`. Neither checks bounds; both are faithful to retail.

So with zero mod rows (WinData/*.pkm parked, as the gate does), the token "1000" reads entries._data[0] of an empty array and dereferences the element pointer it finds there. That is an out-of-bounds read, or a fault on a null _data. Even with rows present, "2000" calls Swap(0,-1) and reads and writes _mods._data[-1].

The retail functions are byte-faithful, and retail has no such caller: the harness comment says so itself. So this is a defect in the harness's input handling, not port drift, and the fix belongs in the harness, not in ModDialog or Modification. No runtime repro was made; the defect follows directly from the unguarded index path above.
verdict.minimal_fix:
In pausemenu_harness.cpp's bare-token branch, before calling OnElementEvent, read `int rows = dlg->entries.GetSize();` and skip the click, logging it, when the id falls in a row range whose row is missing. Each range maps to rows as follows:
- 1000-1999 and 4000-4999: the row is id%1000 and must satisfy 0 <= row < rows.
- 2000-2999 (move up): row = id-2000, and 1 <= row < rows.
- 3000-3999 (move down): row = id-3000, and 0 <= row < rows-1.

This mirrors the autostart.cpp:346-361 guard and the `t<row>` check a few lines above. ModDialog and Modification are faithful and stay unchanged.

confirmed.title: MouseInject::PostUpdate dereferences the target element and dialog after UserInterface::Update may have deleted them
confirmed.bug_class: use-after-free (stale raw pointer across a destroying call)
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: PreUpdate stores raw pointers `g_lastTarget = t.elem; g_lastDlg = t.dlg;` (mouse_inject.cpp:773-774). gameupdateloop.cpp:1162-1164 then runs `MouseInject::PreUpdate(m_userInterface); m_userInterface->Update(*time); MouseInject::PostUpdate(m_userInterface);`. PostUpdate reads `const uint32_t f = g_lastTarget->_flags;` and `g_lastDlg->_hovering` (lines 847-850), and under trace mode also `d->_hoverMouseX/_hoverTime`. UserInterface::Update dispatches the queued click events (UpdateEvents) and then CleanRemovedDialogs #3 (userinterface_frame.cpp:483), which does `delete dlg` (userinterface.cpp:1031) for a dialog a handler closed, and that delete frees its element tree. The press / release / drop steps exist to make retail act on a click, so a release on any element whose handler closes its own dialog (a close button, OK, a pause-menu entry) frees both objects inside Update. The injector also does nothing to steer away from such elements: `#<name>` selects any element by name.
confirmed.repro_idea: With an info panel open (BANISHED_TOOL_HARNESS=housepanel), set BANISHED_MOUSE_INJECT=hover,press,release BANISHED_MOUSE_TARGET=#buttonClose. Under the Linux ASan build, expect heap-use-after-free in MouseInject::PostUpdate on the release frame.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: memory (harness-only, BANISHED_MOUSE_INJECT armed)
verdict.proof:
The finding could not be refuted, and it is not in the ledger: a grep of docs/history/review_20261103 for MouseInject, mouse_inject and g_lastTarget finds nothing about this.

How the stale pointer reaches PostUpdate (all in <worktree>):
1. On each armed frame, PreUpdate clears g_lastTarget and g_lastDlg (mouse_inject.cpp:737-738). For any step other than probe, wait or coord, it then calls FindTarget and stores raw pointers to the target element and its dialog (773-774). This happens before m_userInterface->Update. The game update loop calls PreUpdate, then Update, then PostUpdate in that order (gameupdateloop.cpp:1162-1164).
2. The default hold is 20 frames (mouse_inject.cpp:188). So during a release step the target is found again, and the pointers stored again, on every frame of that step, while the dialog is still alive before Update runs.
3. Inside UserInterface::Update, UpdateEvents() runs first, followed directly by CleanRemovedDialogs() #2 (userinterface_frame.cpp:314-315), and CleanRemovedDialogs() #3 runs at 483. A close handler reached through UpdateEvents goes through UserInterface::CloseDialog, which queues the dialog for removal. FollowDialog shows the path: OnElementEvent with msg 0x12 / id 100 calls Close(), which calls _ui->CloseDialog (followdialog.cpp:245-262). CleanRemovedDialogs then runs `delete dlg` (userinterface.cpp:1031) whenever flag bit 5 is clear. That delete does not depend on the InternalPtr reference count.
4. PostUpdate checks only armed, ui and g_lastTarget, then reads g_lastTarget->_flags and g_lastDlg->_hovering (847-850). With trace on it also reads the dialog's _hoverMouseX/Y and _hoverTime. If the close fired during this frame's Update, all of these reads hit freed memory.

Click events are queued during element update, which runs after UpdateEvents. So the close handler runs at the next frame's UpdateEvents. That next frame is still inside the 20-frame release step, so PreUpdate has just stored the pointers again before Update frees the dialog. The frame offset therefore does not close the window.

Why this is not marked confirmed:
- No sanitizer run backs it yet.
- The repro's specific panel is unverified. It is not shown that the housepanel `#buttonClose` handler goes through CloseDialog and a flag-bit-5-clear delete, rather than hiding a pinned or shared EntityUI panel.
- It is not shown that deleting the dialog frees the element tree that holds the target element.
Running the Linux ASan build with BANISHED_MOUSE_INJECT=hover,press,release and BANISHED_MOUSE_TARGET=#buttonClose on a dialog that is really closed (for example the FollowDialog close button) should report a heap-use-after-free in MouseInject::PostUpdate.
verdict.minimal_fix: Have PostUpdate stop dereferencing pointers it cached before Update. Either re-resolve the target after Update (call FindTarget again and read the flags only if the element is still found), or hold the element and dialog through Object::InternalPtr. The InternalPtr route does not help against CleanRemovedDialogs' unconditional `delete`, so the re-resolve approach is the safe one. Harness-only code; no NOT RETAIL comment is needed.

proof_run.proof:
Confirmed by an instrumented debug run on Windows. The functional game dir C:/GOG Games/Banished-B was taken through tools/game_dirs.sh and released afterwards. WSL / ASan could not be reached from this isolated worktree because the harness refused wsl.exe, so there is no sanitizer report. The evidence is a direct observation that the code reads memory after it was freed.

Instrumentation (proof only, already reverted in the worktree; the diff is saved):
- a stderr line just before `delete dlg` in UI::UserInterface::CleanRemovedDialogs
- a stderr line in MouseInject::PreUpdate where g_lastTarget / g_lastDlg are stored, printing the dialog's vptr
- a stderr line in MouseInject::PostUpdate just before `g_lastTarget->_flags` is read. It prints whether g_lastDlg is still in ui->_dialogs and the dialog's current first qword.

Route: debug build of origin/main fa150cf7f, launched at the front end with:
BANISHED_AUTOMENU_BUTTON=4 (opens Options)
BANISHED_MOUSE_INJECT=hover,press,release,w,w
BANISHED_MOUSE_TARGET=#buttonCancel
BANISHED_MOUSE_START=400
The menu seam (MenuDLT::Stub_Update) runs PreUpdate, then DialogLoopT::Update, then PostUpdate. OptionsDialog's Cancel handler calls _ui->CloseDialog (optionsdialog.cpp:1103/1144).

Observed log (standalone_error.log):
[UAFPROOF] PreUpdate f=441 store g_lastTarget=000001805a1615f0 g_lastDlg=000001805a000370 vptr=00007ff654cdd0e0
[UAFPROOF] CleanRemovedDialogs delete dlg=000001805a000370
[UAFPROOF] PostUpdate f=441 reads g_lastTarget=000001805a1615f0 g_lastDlg=000001805a000370 dlgStillInUiList=0 vptrNow=00000000001633c8

All three lines are from frame 441. The dialog is deleted inside UserInterface::Update, between the store and the read. In PostUpdate it is no longer in the UI's dialog list, and its vptr slot now holds heap free-list data. PostUpdate then goes on to read g_lastTarget->_flags (an element of the deleted dialog) and g_lastDlg->_hovering. With BANISHED_MOUSE_TRACE=1 it would also read _hoverMouseX/Y and _hoverTime. These are reads of freed memory, which is the claimed use-after-free.

The finding's route through the game loop (gameupdateloop.cpp:1162-1164) has the same PreUpdate / Update / PostUpdate shape. This run reproduced the bug through the menu seam (menudialogloopt_stubs.cpp:425-429) and Options Cancel, not through the housepanel close button. The bug is harness-only: nothing happens unless BANISHED_MOUSE_INJECT is set.

Artefacts are in scratchpad/phase2/proofs/mouseinject-postupdate-uaf/:
- uafproof_lines.log
- standalone_error.log
- instrumentation.diff
proof_run.minimal_fix: In MouseInject::PostUpdate (src/diag/mouse_inject.cpp:842-850), do not dereference g_lastTarget / g_lastDlg unless the dialog is still live after Update. Walk ui->_dialogs; if g_lastDlg is not in the list, clear both pointers and return before any read. confirmed.title: Windows hang watchdog walks suspended threads through loader-lock / function-table-lock APIs, so a hang held under the loader lock deadlocks the watchdog and the unattended run never exits 4
confirmed.bug_class: error path deadlocks (lock taken while the lock holder is suspended)
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: WriteHangDump suspends each thread and, while it is still suspended, calls `StandaloneWalkStack(&ctx, &HangStackSink, nullptr);` (line 275, ResumeThread only after). The walker (crash_handler_win.cpp:55-100) calls `GetModuleHandleExA(...FROM_ADDRESS...)` and `GetModuleFileNameA(mod, path, MAX_PATH)` per frame (both take the loader's module lock / loader lock), plus `RtlLookupFunctionEntry` (inverted / dynamic function-table lock) and `IsBadReadPtr`. If the suspended thread holds one of those locks, the watchdog blocks for good. Typical holders are a main thread hung inside LoadLibrary / DllMain (driver or shader-compiler DLL load), or any thread in thread attach/detach. TerminateProcess(…, 4) at line 355 is then never reached and the run sits until the external timeout, which is the failure this file exists to prevent. The Darwin twin (darwin/boot_state_watchdog_darwin.cpp:134-137) already handles this: it captures raw PCs while the thread is suspended and symbolizes only after resuming, with the comment "if the suspended thread holds malloc's or dyld's lock, the watchdog would wait on it forever and never reach _exit(4)". A second instance of the same class: the `std::fprintf(stderr, …)` + `fflush(stderr)` at lines 341-348 runs before the dump and the terminate, so a main thread hung while holding stderr's FILE lock (blocked in a write to a full stderr pipe) stops the watchdog before it can terminate.
confirmed.repro_idea: Make the main thread spin inside a DllMain (a test DLL that loops in DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH, LoadLibrary'd from a diag hook) on an unattended run. Expect no standalone_hang.log beyond the header, no exit 4, and boot_state.sh reporting STALE instead of HUNG. The fix is the Darwin shape: capture RIP/RSP plus raw [RSP] words while suspended, and unwind or symbolize after ResumeThread.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: race (diagnostic harness hang; the unattended run never exits 4)
verdict.proof:
The code matches the description. The finding is not in the ledger: README F-001..F-217, findings_p3p4.json and findings_p8.json have no entry for the hang dump or WriteHangDump, and P0_MAP.md:438 only lists the watchdog's Interlocked flags. Line by line on origin/main (<worktree>):
- boot_state_watchdog.cpp WriteHangDump calls SuspendThread(th), then GetThreadContext, then `StandaloneWalkStack(&ctx, &HangStackSink, nullptr);`. ResumeThread(th) comes only after the walk. This happens for every thread in the process except the watchdog, not only the main thread.
- crash_handler_win.cpp StandaloneWalkStack, for each frame: GetModuleHandleExA(FROM_ADDRESS|UNCHANGED_REFCOUNT), GetModuleFileNameA, RtlLookupFunctionEntry, IsBadReadPtr and RtlVirtualUnwind. Its own comment only covers the CRT FILE lock ("nothing here touches a CRT FILE*: ... a suspended thread can be holding the CRT's file lock"). It says nothing about loader or function-table locks.
- The Darwin twin (src/diag/darwin/boot_state_watchdog_darwin.cpp:135-137) states the same hazard for dyld and malloc locks and avoids it by capturing raw PCs while the thread is suspended and symbolizing after resume. The Windows twin does not do this.
- TerminateProcess(GetCurrentProcess(), 4) runs only after WriteHangDump returns. A watchdog blocked inside the walk therefore never reaches it, and the boot state file stops being rewritten.

What static reading cannot settle is the OS side. Which ntdll and kernelbase locks GetModuleFileNameW and GetModuleHandleExW(FROM_ADDRESS) take on current Windows 10/11 builds (LdrpLoaderLock vs LdrpModuleDatatableLock), and whether RtlLookupFunctionEntry's shared acquire of LdrpInvertedFunctionTableSRWLock can block behind a suspended writer, are undocumented internals that change between builds. So the deadlock is plausible but not airtight. The stderr half is weaker. stderr goes to standalone_error.log, a file and not a pipe, so the main thread would have to be hung while already inside a CRT stderr call.

Proof needed: a diag-hook test. Load a DLL whose DLL_PROCESS_ATTACH spins, on the main thread of an unattended run. Expect standalone_hang.log to stop at the main-thread header with no exit 4 and boot_state.sh reporting STALE, not HUNG/exit 4. Or a unit test: one thread holds the loader lock (LdrLockLoaderLock, or spins in DllMain) and another thread suspends it and calls StandaloneWalkStack on it, under a timeout.
verdict.minimal_fix: Use the Darwin shape in WriteHangDump. While the thread is suspended, call only GetThreadContext and copy RIP/RSP/RBP plus a bounded raw copy of the stack (ReadProcessMemory on the current process, or a fixed number of [RSP] qwords). Call ResumeThread, then run StandaloneWalkStack (module lookup, RtlLookupFunctionEntry/RtlVirtualUnwind) on the copied context, or print raw addresses. Optionally write the HUNG stderr line with WriteFile on GetStdHandle(STD_ERROR_HANDLE) instead of the CRT fprintf, so a stderr FILE lock held by the hung thread cannot block it.

proof_run.proof:
The class is confirmed, but the trigger named in the finding is wrong. The harness is a standalone program built with the pinned WinLibs GCC 16.2 and run on Windows 10 19045. It wraps StandaloneWalkStack from src/diag/win/crash_handler_win.cpp at fa150cf7f, extracted verbatim by awk into walker_extract.inc. It repeats WriteHangDump's sequence (SuspendThread, GetThreadContext, StandaloneWalkStack, ResumeThread) from a watchdog thread that exists before the hang, as in the game. The harness reports completion through an event rather than a thread return, because thread exit takes the loader lock. A run counts as BLOCKED when there is no progress for 10 s.

1) The finding's own repro is REFUTED on this OS. A victim thread holding LdrLockLoaderLock (mode 1), or hung inside a spinning DllMain reached through LoadLibrary (mode 2), does NOT block the walker. The walk COMPLETED in both, with 5 and 17 frames; mode 2 printed spin_dll.dll then the ntdll LdrpCallInitRoutine chain. GetModuleHandleExA(FROM_ADDRESS), GetModuleFileNameA and RtlLookupFunctionEntry do not take LdrpLoaderLock.

2) The deadlock class is CONFIRMED: a lock held by a suspended thread. The victim was a worker thread looping LoadLibraryA / FreeLibrary on a trivial DLL, standing in for any driver or shader-compiler thread loading a module. The watchdog dumped it repeatedly the way WriteHangDump does. The walker deadlocked inside StandaloneWalkStack with the victim suspended in all 5 runs: "RESULT: BLOCKED for 10 s at dump 50 / 927 / 65 / 1867 / ... (stage 2 = inside StandaloneWalkStack with the victim suspended)". The API runs isolate GetModuleFileNameA as the blocker: it BLOCKED at dumps 2868 and 779. GetModuleHandleExA and RtlLookupFunctionEntry on the top RIP alone ran 200000 dumps clean, twice each. The lock is evidently the loader's module-table lock, not LdrpLoaderLock. Once the watchdog blocks, TerminateProcess(..., 4) is never reached, which is the failure the finding describes. In the game this needs any thread other than the hung main thread to be suspended mid LoadLibrary/FreeLibrary when the hang is dumped, so it is a race and not certain on each hang. The stderr half of the finding was not tested.

3) Fix shapes tested:
- The finding's fix, "unwind while suspended, names after resume" (api 4), STILL BLOCKS, and sooner: at dumps 5, 12, 22, 26 and 21 of 5 runs. Unwinding through frames of the DLL being loaded or unloaded (GetModuleHandleExA / RtlLookupFunctionEntry on those PCs) waits on the same lock.
- Walking the live stack after ResumeThread crashed the harness (exit 139 in 2 of 2 runs).
- The Darwin shape (api 5) passed 5 of 5 runs of 200000 dumps each, and modes 1 and 2 also completed. While suspended it does only GetThreadContext, VirtualQuery on RSP and a memcpy of at most 16 KB of raw stack words. After ResumeThread it resolves RIP and every stack word through GetModuleHandleExA + GetModuleFileNameA.

Logs: run.log (verbatim walker), run_api.log (per-API isolation), run_fix.log (api 4 still blocks), run_fix_darwin.log (api 5 never blocks). A bad first harness run, where the watchdog was created after the lock was taken, is superseded by these logs.
proof_run.minimal_fix: In WriteHangDump (src/diag/win/boot_state_watchdog.cpp), between SuspendThread and ResumeThread, call nothing that reaches the loader: GetThreadContext, VirtualQuery(ctx.Rsp) and a bounded memcpy (for example 2048 qwords, clipped to the committed region) of the stack above RSP into a static buffer. ResumeThread, then report RIP and the stack words that GetModuleHandleExA(FROM_ADDRESS) resolves into a module, with names from GetModuleFileNameA, as raw candidate return addresses. This is the Darwin twin's shape. Keeping StandaloneWalkStack's RtlLookupFunctionEntry/RtlVirtualUnwind loop under the suspend, even with names deferred, does not fix it (proved: api 4 blocks). Unwinding after resume against the live stack crashes. A precise unwind would have to run RtlVirtualUnwind on the copied stack with RSP rebased, and with the module and function-table lookups done after resume. The crash-handler path (same-thread walk in the VEH) is unaffected and can keep StandaloneWalkStack. Comment the change as harness hardening (not retail code): "GetModuleFileNameA / GetModuleHandleExA / RtlLookupFunctionEntry wait on the loader's module-table lock; a thread suspended mid LoadLibrary/FreeLibrary holds it". Optionally write the HUNG stderr line with WriteFile(GetStdHandle(STD_ERROR_HANDLE)); that half was not tested.
proof_run.repro_path: scratchpad\phase2\proofs\hang_walk_loader_lock\ (hang_walk_test.cpp, walker_extract.inc, spin_dll.cpp, plain_dll.cpp, run.sh; repro: run.sh 3 0 0 -> BLOCKED; run.sh 3 0 5 -> COMPLETED; logs run.log, run_api.log, run_fix.log, run_fix_darwin.log)

confirmed.title: POSIX/Android hang dump: a late per-thread answer is consumed by the next thread's wait and can write into a closed or reused fd
confirmed.bug_class: error path continues with stale state (semaphore count drift, fd TOCTOU)
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: For each thread: `syscall(SYS_tgkill, pid, tid, kDumpSignal)`, then `sem_timedwait(&g_dumpDone, &deadline)` with a 1 s deadline (line 201). On timeout the loop moves on, but the signal stays pending: the handler (line 143-148) still runs DumpOwnStack and `sem_post(&g_dumpDone)` later, when the thread unblocks. That stale post satisfies the next thread's sem_timedwait at once, so the following stacks are attributed to the wrong `--- thread N ---` headers or interleave. The count also carries into the next hang dump of the same process (hungReported resets when frames move again). After the loop, `close(g_hangLog); g_hangLog = -1;` (line 209) races a still-running handler that already passed `if (g_hangLog < 0 ...)` in HangLogRaw. On an attended run the watchdog keeps going, and its next `fopen("standalone_boot_state.txt","w")` can reuse that fd number, so stack lines land in the machine-read state file. The same code is at android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp:219/227.
confirmed.repro_idea: Linux attended run (no BANISHED_UNATTENDED): one thread blocks the dump signal for 2 s (pthread_sigmask around a sleep) while the main loop is frozen for more than 20 s. Check standalone_hang.log for the next thread's header followed by the first thread's frames, and check the next standalone_boot_state.txt for stray '#N' lines.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: low (diagnostic hang log only, attended or unattended; no sim/save effect). The fd-reuse half is overstated.
verdict.proof:
Not in the ledger: no hit for boot_state_watchdog_posix/android, g_dumpDone, sem_timedwait or "hang dump" under docs/history/review_20261103/. Not fixed on origin/main either (<worktree>).

The stale post can be checked line by line in src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp:
- g_dumpDone is a counting semaphore that never gets drained (sem_init(&g_dumpDone,0,0) at :313). Every thread posts to the same semaphore, and nothing records which thread posted (DumpSignalHandler :144-149).
- WriteHangDump (:194-202) sends tgkill to thread A and waits on sem_timedwait with a 1 s deadline. The code expects that wait to time out sometimes: it writes "(no answer within 1s: blocked with the signal masked?)" at :202.
- On a timeout the signal stays pending or is still running. When A's handler finishes later it posts once. That post is still unconsumed when the loop has moved on to thread B. B's sem_timedwait then returns at once on A's token, the loop moves to thread C while B's handler may still be writing frames, and stacks from A, B and C interleave or land under the wrong "--- thread N ---" header (HangLogRaw writes lines with no lock and no thread identity).
- Any token left over survives the function. On an attended run hungReported resets when frames advance (:226-230). A second HUNG then reuses the same semaphore, and its first wait is satisfied by the old token.
- The same structure is in src/diag/android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp:165/219/227/330.

The close/fd-reuse claim is mostly refuted. HangLogRaw and HangLogf re-read g_hangLog on every line (:100, :110). After `close; g_hangLog = -1` (:209-210), a late handler writes nothing more unless it was preempted exactly between loading g_hangLog and the write() syscall. The next fopen("standalone_boot_state.txt") comes only after usleep(1s) (:284), so for stack lines to reach the state file, a handler would have to stay preempted inside that window for more than a second. Another thread's open() could reuse the fd sooner, but the window is still a single load-to-syscall gap. Plain int with no atomic is technically a data race, but it is not the practical failure described.

Reachability: it needs a thread that answers more than 1 s late (signal masked, sleeping in an uninterruptible syscall, or a slow dladdr/backtrace on a loaded machine). The code's own timeout message admits this case.
verdict.minimal_fix: Make each answer identifiable and drop stale tokens. Before each tgkill, drain leftover posts (`while (sem_trywait(&g_dumpDone) == 0) {}`), and set an atomic g_dumpTarget = tid. In the handler, write and post only if `CurrentTid() == g_dumpTarget`; otherwise return. After a timeout, set g_dumpTarget = 0 so a late handler does nothing. Make g_hangLog a std::atomic<int>. Apply the same change to android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp. Title: "fix: hang dump ignores a late per-thread answer (POSIX/Android watchdog)".

confirmed.title: BANISHED_STRESS_SETS=-2147483648 negates INT_MIN (signed overflow)
confirmed.bug_class: UB (signed overflow) from env input
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: options.cpp:182 reads `o.stressSets = Int("BANISHED_STRESS_SETS", …)` through ClampedAtoi, which clamps to [INT_MIN, INT_MAX], and line 201 keeps negative values on purpose ("stressSets < 0 is kept"). stress_harness.cpp:1591 has `return s_enabled == 1 ? (s_sets < 0 ? -s_sets : s_sets) : 0;` and the same `-s_sets` appears at line 1313 in the CSV header. With s_sets == INT_MIN, `-s_sets` is undefined behaviour, and the result feeds StartTown_StressSpawnStructures' `sets` (starttown.cpp:1154). This is not F-087: the parse is already clamped, and the overflow is in the arithmetic afterwards.
confirmed.repro_idea: Run under UBSan (WSL): BANISHED_STRESS=1 BANISHED_STRESS_SETS=-2147483648. Expect 'negation of -2147483648 cannot be represented in type int' at stress_harness.cpp:1591. A minimal fix clamps stressSets to > INT_MIN in options.cpp, with a NOT RETAIL: comment.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: UB (low; harness-only env input)
verdict.proof:
The finding could not be refuted. Each step below can be checked line by line in <worktree>:
(1) src/app/options.cpp:37-40: Int() returns ClampedAtoi(v). src/app/clamped_atoi.h:14-21 uses strtoll and clamps to [INT_MIN, INT_MAX]. "-2147483648", or any smaller value such as "-9999999999", therefore comes back as exactly INT_MIN.
(2) options.cpp:182 stores that value in o.stressSets. The post-clamp block (options.cpp:200-205) clamps stressCitizens, stressInterval and stressSpeed but deliberately leaves stressSets alone (line 201: "stressSets < 0 is kept").
(3) src/diag/stress_harness.cpp:156-159 Resolve(): when Opt().stress is set (BANISHED_STRESS=1), s_enabled = 1 and s_sets = Opt().stressSets = INT_MIN, with no further check.
(4) stress_harness.cpp:1591 StressHarness_Sets() evaluates `s_sets < 0 ? -s_sets : s_sets` while s_enabled == 1, so it computes -INT_MIN in int. That is signed overflow, which is undefined behaviour ([expr.pre]/4; UBSan reports "negation of -2147483648 cannot be represented in type 'int'"). The same expression appears at stress_harness.cpp:1313 (OpenCsv, the CSV header line), which runs whenever the CSV opens.
The ledger has no duplicate. A grep for stress_harness / STRESS_SETS / stressSets / s_sets in docs/history/review_20261103 (README.md, P0_MAP.md, findings_p3p4.json, findings_p8.json) finds only an unrelated buffer-offset note. F-087 covers only the atoi parse, which is now clamped; this overflow happens in the arithmetic after it. The code is a diagnostics harness, so there is no retail or port-drift question. A UBSan run would only demonstrate the same line again; it is not needed to establish the defect.
verdict.minimal_fix: In src/app/options.cpp, after line 201, add `if (o.stressSets == INT_MIN) o.stressSets = INT_MIN + 1;` with a comment such as `// NOT RETAIL: -INT_MIN overflows in StressHarness_Sets / OpenCsv (review)`. Include <climits> if it is not already pulled in through clamped_atoi.h. Alternatively, compute the magnitude once in Resolve() using an unsigned or clamped value. Either way, both use sites (stress_harness.cpp:1313 and :1591) are covered.

confirmed.title: BANISHED_REDZONE_PAD near INT_MAX overflows `redzonePad + 7` (signed overflow)
confirmed.bug_class: UB (signed overflow) from env input
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: `if (Opt().redzonePad > 0) g_pad = (size_t)((Opt().redzonePad + 7) & ~7);  // 8-byte multiple`. redzonePad is an int parsed from the environment (clamped to INT_MAX by ClampedAtoi), so for any value above INT_MAX-7 `+ 7` is a signed overflow before the cast. Even without the overflow, a huge pad goes unchecked into `g_realAlloc(size + g_pad, alignment)` (line 204) and `memset(CanaryPtr(p, size), kCanary, g_pad)`.
confirmed.repro_idea: BANISHED_REDZONE=1 BANISHED_REDZONE_PAD=2147483647 under a -fsanitize=signed-integer-overflow Windows build (LLVM toolchain in C:/winlibs-gcc16-llvm). Or reduce: a unit test of the expression with INT_MAX. Fix: do the arithmetic in size_t / int64 and cap the pad.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: UB (signed overflow), harness-only: needs BANISHED_REDZONE set and BANISHED_REDZONE_PAD > INT_MAX-7
verdict.proof:
The steps below can each be checked against origin/main in <worktree>.
(1) src/app/options.cpp:221 reads `o.redzonePad = Int("BANISHED_REDZONE_PAD", 0);`. Int() (line 39) returns `v ? ClampedAtoi(v) : dflt`.
(2) src/app/clamped_atoi.h: ClampedAtoi parses with strtoll and returns INT_MAX for any v > INT_MAX. So BANISHED_REDZONE_PAD=2147483647 (or any larger number) gives redzonePad == INT_MAX, and 2147483641..2147483647 all reach the overflow range.
(3) src/diag/win/redzone_alloc.cpp:337 is `if (Opt().redzonePad > 0) g_pad = (size_t)((Opt().redzonePad + 7) & ~7);`. The guard INT_MAX > 0 holds. `Opt().redzonePad + 7` is int + int, so it is computed in int before the cast to size_t, and INT_MAX - 6 .. INT_MAX + 7 cannot be represented. That is signed overflow, undefined behaviour under [expr.pre]/4. The size_t cast comes after the overflow and does not save it.
Nothing else clamps redzonePad: options.cpp has no range check after line 221, and nothing else reads the field.
Follow-on effects, not needed for the UB claim: a huge g_pad goes unchecked into `g_realAlloc(size + g_pad, ...)` (line 204) and `memset(..., g_pad)` (line 216). Line 123 also does `(int)g_pad`, which narrows a large pad.
Ledger check: no redzone or REDZONE_PAD finding in README.md (F-001..F-217), P0_MAP.md, findings_p3p4.json or findings_p8.json. The only redzone mention in findings_p3p4.json cites line 144 as an example of correct code. Not fixed on origin/main: line 337 is unchanged.
verdict.minimal_fix: src/diag/win/redzone_alloc.cpp:337: do the rounding in size_t, for example `if (Opt().redzonePad > 0) g_pad = ((size_t)Opt().redzonePad + 7) & ~size_t(7);  // NOT RETAIL: size_t arithmetic, no int overflow on a huge BANISHED_REDZONE_PAD`. Optionally add a sane cap (for example 1 MiB) as plain hardening, so that size + g_pad and the line-123 `(int)g_pad` stay in range.

confirmed.title: BANISHED_FINGER_TAP hold = INT_MAX overflows `s_ft_hold + 1` on every tick
confirmed.bug_class: UB (signed overflow) from env input
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: ArmFingerTap: `std::sscanf(e, "%f,%f,%d,%d", &fx, &fy, &delay, &hold); s_ft_hold = hold > 0 ? hold : 1; s_ft_frame = frameNum + (delay > 0 ? delay : 1);`. FingerTapTick line 991: `if (s_ft_frame < 0 || s_ft_step > s_ft_hold + 1 || frameNum < s_ft_frame + s_ft_step) return;` and line 995 `const bool up = s_ft_step == s_ft_hold + 1;`. An in-range hold of 2147483647 (no sscanf overflow involved, so not covered by F-087) makes `s_ft_hold + 1` overflow every frame, and a delay near INT_MAX overflows `frameNum + delay`.
confirmed.repro_idea: UBSan run with BANISHED_FINGER_TAP=0.5,0.5,30,2147483647 and the harness route that arms it (tools/device_sim.sh).

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: minor
verdict.proof:
I tried to refute this and could not. The code on origin/main (<worktree>/src/diag/tool_harness.cpp:969-1011) matches the finding.

How the hold overflows:
1. ArmFingerTap parses BANISHED_FINGER_TAP with `sscanf("%f,%f,%d,%d")`. For the input `0.5,0.5,30,2147483647`, the value 2147483647 fits in an int, so sscanf has no out-of-range conversion here.
2. `s_ft_hold = hold > 0 ? hold : 1` sets s_ft_hold to INT_MAX.
3. `s_ft_frame = frameNum + 30` is non-negative, so the tap is armed.
4. On every later call, FingerTapTick line 991 checks `s_ft_frame < 0` first. That is false, so the `||` chain goes on to evaluate `s_ft_step > s_ft_hold + 1`, which is INT_MAX + 1 in int. That is signed overflow, which is UB. Nothing clamps the value earlier.
5. Line 993 (`s_ft_step == s_ft_hold + 1`, given as 995 in the finding) does the same addition again once frameNum reaches s_ft_frame.

The delay has the same problem. With delay = INT_MAX - k and frameNum > k, `frameNum + delay` in ArmFingerTap (line 984) overflows. Later, `s_ft_frame + s_ft_step` on line 991 can also overflow.

In practice, an optimiser may treat `s_ft_step > s_ft_hold + 1` as always false. The finger then stays down forever and never sends the up event, which is a real behaviour change and not only a theoretical one.

Ledger check: neither README.md (F-001..F-217), P0_MAP.md nor findings_p3p4.json / findings_p8.json mentions FINGER_TAP, FingerTap or s_ft_. F-087 covers atoi out-of-range conversions in main.cpp, not arithmetic after a valid sscanf parse. So this is not a duplicate.

The label is harness: Opt().fingerTap is a harness flag set by tools/device_sim.sh, so the code is not faithful game code and has no retail counterpart.
verdict.minimal_fix:
Clamp the inputs in ArmFingerTap so that none of the later additions can overflow. Use plain hardening; no NOT RETAIL comment is needed because this is harness code:
- `s_ft_hold = hold > 0 ? std::min(hold, 1 << 20) : 1;`
- `const int d = delay > 0 ? std::min(delay, 1 << 20) : 1;`
- `s_ft_frame = frameNum + d;`
Alternatively, compute in int64_t / long long in both ArmFingerTap and FingerTapTick.

confirmed.title: Hang dump: a thread that answers kDumpSignal after the 1 s timeout posts the shared semaphore late (shifting every later thread's wait) and its handler can write to g_hangLog after WriteHangDump closed it, i.e. into whatever file next reuses that fd number
confirmed.bug_class: dangling fd / cross-thread signal-handler race (late sem_post on a shared counting semaphore)
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: SUSPECTED (static only). The handler is `void DumpSignalHandler(int, siginfo_t*, void* ucv) { ... DumpInterruptedStack(uc->uc_mcontext); sem_post(&g_dumpDone); ... }` (:161-167). It writes through `HangLogRaw`: `if (g_hangLog < 0 || !s) return; ssize_t r = write(g_hangLog, s, std::strlen(s));` (:93-97). The watchdog does `syscall(SYS_tgkill, pid, tid, kDumpSignal)` and then `if (sem_timedwait(&g_dumpDone, &deadline) != 0) HangLogRaw("  (no answer within 1s: ...)\n");` (:212-220). It moves on to the next tid without draining or tagging the answer, and finally runs `fsync(g_hangLog); close(g_hangLog); g_hangLog = -1;` (:226-228). g_dumpDone is a counting semaphore shared by every thread. When thread A answers after its 1 s deadline, its sem_post satisfies thread B's wait, so B's frames (and A's) land under the wrong '--- thread ---' header or after END HANG. If A's handler reads g_hangLog between close() and the -1 store, or after the descriptor number has been reused by an open on another thread (attended runs keep running after a HUNG: only `Opt().unattendedBoot` calls _exit(4)), its write(2) goes into an unrelated file, such as a save temp file or the settings .tmp. g_hangLog is also a plain int read from the signal handler on another thread, which is a data race. The POSIX twin has the same shape (src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp:95-112, :147, :201, :208-210). The ledger has no entry for it.
confirmed.repro_idea: In a debug build, make one thread stall in an uninterruptible wait longer than 1 s (for example a write on an O_SYNC fd to slow storage, or stop it with ptrace) while the main loop is stalled 20 s with the attended watchdog. Have that thread's dump handler sleep 1.5 s before sem_post. Show that the next thread's section is empty or misattributed, and that the late write lands in a file opened right after the dump (open a file in a loop on another thread and grep it for '  #0 ').

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: low (diagnostic-only path; output misattribution is likely once triggered, a stray write into a reused fd needs an attended run plus a late delivery)
verdict.proof:
The finding holds. Every step can be checked line by line in <worktree>/src/diag/android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp, and the POSIX twin src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp is the same.

What the code does:
1. g_dumpDone is a single counting semaphore, created once with `sem_init(&g_dumpDone, 0, 0)` (:330; POSIX :313). The same semaphore serves every thread and every dump.
2. For each tid, WriteHangDump does `syscall(SYS_tgkill, pid, tid, kDumpSignal)` and then `if (sem_timedwait(&g_dumpDone, &deadline) != 0) HangLogRaw("  (no answer within 1s...")` (:212-220).
   - On a timeout the code never drains or cancels the answer that is still owed.
   - Nothing in the semaphore says which thread posted.
3. kDumpSignal is SIGRTMIN+3, a real-time signal. RT signals stay queued: a tgkill to a thread that has the signal masked, or that is in uninterruptible sleep, is delivered whenever that thread next unmasks it or returns to user mode. That can be any time after the 1 s deadline. When it arrives, DumpSignalHandler (:161-167) runs DumpInterruptedStack, writes through HangLogRaw/g_hangLog (:93-97) and calls sem_post.

Result A (misattribution):
- The late sem_post makes the semaphore count one too high, so a later thread's sem_timedwait returns at once.
- That later thread's frames then land under a following header, or after "=== END HANG ===".
- A late frame write can also interleave with the watchdog's own header writes, because both write to the same fd at the same time.
- The extra count survives past the dump. hungReported resets when frames move again (:245-248), so it also corrupts the first wait of any later dump.

Result B (stray write into another file):
- After the loop the watchdog runs `fsync; close(g_hangLog); g_hangLog = -1;` (:226-228).
- A handler that is still pending can check `g_hangLog < 0` before the -1 store and write after close(). Once another thread's open() reuses that fd number, the frame text goes into an unrelated file.
- An attended run keeps going after a HUNG; only the unattended path calls _exit(4) (:281), so other threads are still opening files.
- g_hangLog is a plain int that the handler on another thread reads while the watchdog writes it. That is a formal data race.

Ledger check: nothing on this in docs/history/review_20261103. The grep for hang dump / g_dumpDone / kDumpSignal / watchdog only hits the P0_MAP inventory line (:438) and unrelated findings_p8 entries.

Reachability: there is no unit test. The only precondition is an RT signal arriving more than 1 s late, which is standard kernel behaviour for a masked thread or a thread in D state. During a hang (often I/O stalls) that is plausible. Still, a hang-dump repro run would be needed to show the stray write into another file actually happening.

The code is our own diagnostic and has no retail counterpart, so it does not touch sim or save bytes.
verdict.minimal_fix:
Give each request a generation number:
- Add `std::atomic<int> g_hangLog` and `std::atomic<uint32_t> g_dumpGen` (lock-free, so safe to touch in a signal handler).
- Before each tgkill, set the generation for that tid.
- The handler takes `g_hangLog.load()` once. It writes only if the fd is >= 0 and the generation still matches its tid (pass the tid via sigqueue/rt_tgsigqueueinfo si_value, or compare gettid() with the published target), and posts only in that case.
- After a timeout, set the target to 0 so a late handler writes nothing and does not post. Drain any leftover count with `while (sem_trywait(&g_dumpDone) == 0) {}` before each tgkill.
- At the end, store -1 into g_hangLog before close(). To avoid fd reuse in an attended run, either keep the fd open (dup2 /dev/null onto it after the dump) or skip close() for the life of the process.

Apply the same change to src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp.

confirmed.title: Hang dump: a thread that answers the dump signal after the 1 s timeout posts the semaphore late and writes through g_hangLog with no synchronisation, after the watchdog may have closed the fd (the fd number can be reused)
confirmed.bug_class: race / data race on a plain int read in a signal handler on another thread (formally UB); stale semaphore count
confirmed.label: harness
confirmed.evidence: WriteHangDump: `if (sem_timedwait(&g_dumpDone, &deadline) != 0) HangLogRaw("  (no answer within 1s ...)\n");` then moves on to the next tid. After the loop: `fsync(g_hangLog); close(g_hangLog); g_hangLog = -1;` (:226-228). The handler on the target thread: `DumpInterruptedStack(uc->uc_mcontext); sem_post(&g_dumpDone);` (:164-165), and each DumpFrame -> HangLogRaw reads the plain `int g_hangLog` (:89, :94-95). A thread that takes the signal late (blocked in a non-restartable kernel wait, or a signal queued behind a masked section) causes two problems. (1) Its sem_post satisfies the NEXT thread's sem_timedwait at once, so that thread's stack is interleaved with or missing from the log, and the misattribution cascades. (2) If it runs after the loop, it reads g_hangLog concurrently with the watchdog's close()/store of -1 (a non-atomic cross-thread access, UB), and a value read just before the store names a closed fd. In an attended run the process continues (no _exit(4)), so another thread may already have reused that fd number (a save file, the pipe of Readable). The late frames are then written into it. The POSIX twin has the same code (src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp:95-112, :147, :201, :208-210).
confirmed.repro_idea: Unit or harness test: start the watchdog with an extra thread that blocks kDumpSignal (pthread_sigmask) and unblocks it 1.5 s after the HUNG dump starts. Hold the main loop with BANISHED_* unattended off so that HUNG fires. Check standalone_hang.log for the next thread's section showing no stack or the wrong stack. Under TSan on the Linux twin, the late handler's read of g_hangLog races the watchdog's `g_hangLog = -1`. Minimal fix: make g_hangLog std::atomic<int>, drain stale posts with sem_trywait before each tgkill, and tag each answer with the tid it answers for.

verdict.label: harness
verdict.severity: low (diagnostic-only path: runs only after a HUNG verdict; the unattended run _exit(4)s right after)
verdict.proof: The code reads as the finding says (<worktree>/src/diag/android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp). `int g_hangLog` (:89) is a plain int. The signal handler reads it on the target thread through DumpFrame -> HangLogRaw (:94-95, :140, :164). WriteHangDump on the watchdog thread waits for an answer with `sem_timedwait` and a 1 s deadline (:216-220). On a timeout it logs a line and moves on to the next tid, with no drain of the semaphore and no tid tag on the answer. After the loop it runs `fsync; close(g_hangLog); g_hangLog = -1;` (:226-228), with no fence and no atomic. So if a handler runs more than 1 s after its tgkill: (1) its sem_post satisfies a later thread's wait, so that thread's frames can interleave with another's or be cut short; (2) if it runs after the loop, its read of g_hangLog races the watchdog's store of -1 (a cross-thread data race on a non-atomic int, formally UB). A value read between close() and the store names a closed fd, which another thread may already have reused in an attended run that keeps going. The ledger does not cover it: grep of docs/history/review_20261103 for watchdog / hang.log / g_hangLog / sem_timedwait finds only P0_MAP.md:438, the inventory line, and no finding. origin/main has no fix (the file as read). The finding is not airtight because everything depends on late delivery. Nothing in the tree masks kDumpSignal (SIGRTMIN+3, which the comment says is chosen to avoid SDL, bionic and the crash handler). A thread in an interruptible kernel wait takes the signal at once (SA_RESTART restarts the call afterwards), so the finding's 'non-restartable kernel wait' case is not delayed delivery. Delivery waits only on a thread in uninterruptible sleep (D state, for example blocking storage I/O or fsync) or a stopped or traced thread. The handler's own walk (a pipe() and write() per frame through Readable, dladdr) is slow but runs before sem_post, so it delays the answer rather than misattributing it. Whether such a late answer occurs in practice, and whether TSan reports the g_hangLog race, needs the proposed harness: a thread that holds kDumpSignal masked and unmasks it 1.5 s into the dump, run under TSan on the POSIX twin (src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp, the same shape). The harness has to use pthread_sigmask, because the code never masks the signal itself. The fd-reuse leg also needs the read to land in the few-instruction window between close() and the store; after the store HangLogRaw returns early.
verdict.minimal_fix: Make g_hangLog a std::atomic<int> (a lock-free load inside the handler is async-signal-safe). Before close(), exchange it to -1 and close the old value, so no late handler can see a closed fd number. Drain stale posts with sem_trywait before each tgkill, or tag each answer with the tid it answers (an atomic answeredTid that the handler sets before sem_post and the waiter checks). Apply the same change to the POSIX and Darwin twins. Add a NOT RETAIL comment only if the campaign's UB ruling is applied: this is harness code with no retail counterpart.

proof_run.proof:
The finding is confirmed in two ways: a harness run that shows the failure, and a ThreadSanitizer report.

**Setup.** The harness builds the unchanged src/diag/posix/boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp at fa150cf7f (origin/main) under WSL with g++ 13.3. It includes the .cpp to reach WriteHangDump, which sits in an anonymous namespace, and uses stub options.h and topology.h. The worktree itself was not changed. The harness starts three threads in this order:
- **late_L** blocks kDumpSignal with pthread_sigmask, then unblocks it 1.5 s after the dump starts.
- **victim_V** blocks kDumpSignal until the dump has ended.
- **dumper** calls WriteHangDump.

**Failure seen in the plain -O1 -g build** (plain.log, exit 1). In standalone_hang.log:
- late_L's section correctly says "(no answer within 1s ...)".
- victim_V's section has **no** "no answer" line, even though victim_V never answered. late_L's late sem_post at about 1.5 s satisfied victim_V's 1 s wait.
- late_L's backtrace is written under the victim_V header: `--- thread 629 (victim_V) ---` followed by `#5 h + 0x3710 (LateBody+0x29)`.
- After the dump, sem_getvalue(g_dumpDone) = 1 instead of 0. The stale post survives into the next dump, so a later dump can misattribute the same way.
- The harness prints RESULT: FAIL (3).

**TSan build** (tsan.log, exit 66, 2 warnings):
- "WARNING: ThreadSanitizer: data race ... Read of size 4 by main thread: HangLogRaw boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp:100 <- DumpOwnStack :140 <- DumpSignalHandler :146 ... Previous write of size 4 by thread T4: WriteHangDump boot_state_watchdog_posix.cpp:153 ... Location is global 'BootState::(anonymous namespace)::g_hangLog'". The plain int g_hangLog is read in the signal handler on another thread with no synchronisation. The same plain int is later set to -1 at :210.
- A second race: write() through that fd in the handler (:101) against the open() on the watchdog thread (:153).

**Limits of the proof.**
- The fd-reuse leg (a handler reading the fd number between close() and `g_hangLog = -1`) was not hit. That window is a few instructions wide. In the plain run, victim_V's post-loop handler saw -1 and returned early.
- Late delivery needs the signal to be masked or the thread to be in uninterruptible sleep. The harness forces it with pthread_sigmask, because the tree never masks kDumpSignal itself.
- The Android twin (src/diag/android/boot_state_watchdog_android.cpp:89-228) has the same g_hangLog, sem_timedwait and close shape. It was not built here.

Severity is low: this is a diagnostic-only path after a HUNG verdict.
proof_run.minimal_fix:
Apply the same change to the POSIX, Android and Darwin twins:
- Make g_hangLog a std::atomic<int>. A lock-free load is async-signal-safe.
- HangLogRaw and HangLogf load it once into a local and write through that local.
- At the end of WriteHangDump, `const int fd = g_hangLog.exchange(-1); fsync(fd); close(fd);` so no late handler can see a closed fd number.
- Before each tgkill, drain stale posts with `while (sem_trywait(&g_dumpDone) == 0) {}`.
- Have the handler publish its tid to an atomic `g_answeredTid` before sem_post. The waiter accepts a post only when the tid matches; otherwise it waits again until the same deadline.

This is harness code with no retail counterpart. Add a NOT RETAIL comment only to mark the UB fix, per the campaign ruling.
